title: Torus and simple Weyl relations present the split torus normalizer
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $P=(G,T=D_A(M),\Phi,\Phi^\vee,\Delta,(X_\alpha))$ a pinned split realization [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Use the root subgroups $U_\gamma$, exponentials $\exp_\gamma$, Weyl representatives $n_\alpha$, reflections $s_\alpha$, orders $m_{\alpha\beta}$, torus elements $t_{\alpha\beta}$ and positive two-root subgroups $U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}$ of [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus]. An affine $A$-group scheme is an affine scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams; all homomorphisms below preserve those operations. Let $H$ be such a group. Let $N=N_G(T)$ denote the normalizer subgroup scheme: its points normalize $T$ after every further algebra extension. Give a homomorphism $f_T:T\to H$ and sections $h_\alpha\in H(A)$. Suppose, on every commutative $A$-algebra $R$, that $$h_\alpha f_T(t)h_\alpha^{-1}=f_T(s_\alpha(t)),\quad h_\alpha^2=f_T(\alpha^\vee(-1)),\quad (h_\alpha h_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}=f_T(t_{\alpha\beta})$$ for $t\in T(R)$ and distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Delta$. Then there is a unique homomorphism $f_N:N\to H$ with $f_N|_T=f_T$ and $f_N(n_\alpha)=h_\alpha$. If $n=n_{\alpha_1}\cdots n_{\alpha_k}$ and $t\in T(R)$, its value is $f_N(tn)=f_T(t)h_{\alpha_1}\cdots h_{\alpha_k}$. These formulas agree on all presentations of an element and define morphisms on the open-and-closed cosets $Tn$ of $N$. Empty $\Delta$, disconnected and nonreduced $A$, and all residue characteristics are allowed.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus], the quotient sheaf $N/T$ is the constant finite Weyl group $W_A$. Choose for every $w\in W$ a simple-reflection word and its lift $n_w\in N(A)$, choosing the empty word for $1$. The quotient map $q:N\to W_A=\coprod_{w\in W}\operatorname{Spec}A$ has fibre $Tn_w$: for any test scheme, $q(g)=w$ means precisely $gn_w^{-1}\in\ker(q)=T$. This equality is an equality of sheaves, hence of represented functors; translation by $n_w$ identifies that fibre with $T$. Therefore these translates are disjoint open-and-closed subschemes covering $N$. A point of $N(R)$ may have different Weyl labels on different open-and-closed pieces of $\operatorname{Spec}R$; we do not assume it is globally one torus times one word.

proof.text: Fix a nonzero commutative $A$-algebra $R$ and put $E_R=\bigcup_{w\in W}T(R)n_w\subseteq N(R)$, the subgroup with constant Weyl label. Form the abstract group $Q_R$ from symbols $[t]$ for $t\in T(R)$ and $x_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in\Delta$, by imposing $[1]=1$, $[t][u]=[tu]$, and $$x_\alpha[t]x_\alpha^{-1}=[s_\alpha(t)],\quad x_\alpha^2=[\alpha^\vee(-1)],\quad (x_\alpha x_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}=[t_{\alpha\beta}].$$ This means words modulo the congruence generated by these equations and their inverses, so a generator assignment satisfying them descends by evaluating words. The calculus node says that $[t]\mapsto t$, $x_\alpha\mapsto n_\alpha$ satisfies all equations, giving a surjection $p_R:Q_R\to E_R$. Write $j_R(t)=[t]$. It is injective because $p_Rj_R$ is the inclusion $T(R)\hookrightarrow E_R$. Its image is normal: the displayed conjugation equation and $s_\alpha^2=1$ show that conjugation by $x_\alpha$ and its inverse preserves that image; the torus symbols also preserve it.

proof.text: Killing $j_R(T(R))$ in this presentation leaves exactly the generators $x_\alpha$ with square and pair-product Coxeter relations. By [lem-sfb-based-root-datum-coxeter-presentation], the resulting quotient is $W$, with $x_\alpha\mapsto s_\alpha$. Explicitly the maps in both directions send corresponding generators to one another, and are inverse since those generators generate. If $p_R(z)=1$, the image of $z$ in this $W$ is $1$, so $z=j_R(t)$ for some $t\in T(R)$; then $1=p_R(z)=t$ and $z=1$. Thus $p_R$ is an isomorphism. This proves that the torus conjugation and the specified lifted Coxeter relations supply every relation in $E_R$; it does not replace the nontrivial torus extension by a semidirect product.

proof.text: Send the generators of $Q_R$ to $[t]\mapsto f_T(t)$ and $x_\alpha\mapsto h_\alpha$. The internal torus equations hold because $f_T$ is a homomorphism, and each remaining defining equation is exactly a hypothesis of the item after base change to $R$. Word evaluation therefore gives $Q_R\to H(R)$, and composing with $p_R^{-1}$ gives a homomorphism $F_R:E_R\to H(R)$. On any expression $t n_{\alpha_1}\cdots n_{\alpha_k}$ it is $f_T(t)h_{\alpha_1}\cdots h_{\alpha_k}$. Every such expression lifts to the corresponding word in $Q_R$, so the isomorphism just proved makes the formula independent of the expression. Under a homomorphism $R\to R'$, the assignments on every generator commute with base change, hence so do their evaluations. For the zero algebra all scheme-point sets are singletons, and evaluation is uniquely compatible.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, first normalizer-map paragraph; explicit abstract-group argument supplied by Q113, using Milne Appendix C.11 instead of a forbidden source. Local archival Conrad PDF WANTED.

proof.text: For the chosen word for $w$, write $h_w$ for the corresponding product. On the open-and-closed translate $Tn_w$, use the morphism $t n_w\mapsto f_T(t)h_w$: translation, $f_T$, and multiplication by the section $h_w$ are $A$-morphisms. These morphisms glue on the disjoint cover to $f_N:N\to H$. On $Tn_w\times_A Tn_v$ its compatibility with multiplication follows from $F_R$ being a homomorphism: every pair of $R$-points of this component lies in $E_R$. Taking the universal point of this affine component verifies equality of the two scheme morphisms. These components cover $N\times_A N$, proving the group law globally; the identity and inverse follow as well. The word formulas give the required restrictions and values. Any other homomorphism with those values agrees on every $Tn_w$, hence is equal to $f_N$. The same formulas cover arbitrary Weyl words by step 4. If $\Delta$ is empty, $W=1$, $N=T$ and this is just $f_T$; nothing required $A$ or $R$ to be connected, reduced, or of a specified characteristic.
